title: El Niño Is Back After Three Years. India's Monsoon Is Forecast Below Normal for the First Time Since 2023.
excerpt: IMD projects 92% of average rainfall. Skymet says 94%. Both forecasts point to trouble for agriculture, food prices, and India's 7.7% growth story.
body:
India's southwest monsoon is forecast to deliver below-normal rainfall this year, the first such forecast in three years. The India Meteorological Department projects seasonal rainfall at 92 percent of the long-period average, while private forecaster Skymet estimates 94 percent — both firmly in the "below normal" band that tends to strain agriculture, inflate food prices, and drag on economic growth.

The culprit is El Niño, which is expected to develop during the early phase of the monsoon after a year and a half of La Niña conditions. It is the first El Niño emergence since 2023, and forecasters warn it will keep growing stronger through autumn. El Niño — the periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific — disrupts the moisture-laden winds that India's kharif crop cycle depends on. Every major El Niño year since 2000 has coincided with depressed agricultural output.

## What the Numbers Mean for Agriculture

The monsoon irrigates roughly 52 percent of India's net sown area. Agriculture employs over 40 percent of the country's workforce and accounts for 17 to 20 percent of GDP. A shortfall of even 6 to 8 percent in seasonal rainfall can translate into billions of dollars in crop losses, reduced rural incomes, and a surge in wholesale food prices.

Skymet's regional forecast makes the picture sharper. The core monsoon zone — central and western India, where rainfed farming dominates — is expected to receive inadequate rainfall. Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan are likely to see below-normal rain, particularly during August and September, the months that determine the fate of paddy and cotton harvests. Eastern and northeastern states will fare better, but they contribute a smaller share of total grain output.

The Indian Ocean Dipole, which can partially counteract El Niño when it turns strongly positive, is expected to remain neutral or only slightly positive this season. That removes a key buffer that helped protect the 2023 monsoon despite El Niño.

## The Macro Headwinds Stack Up

The monsoon forecast arrives at a difficult moment. India's economy grew 7.7 percent in FY26, its fastest expansion in two years, driven by manufacturing strength and robust investment. But every major forecaster has flagged the monsoon as a swing variable for FY27.

The Reserve Bank of India has already cut its FY27 growth projection to 6.6 percent, raising its inflation forecast to 5.1 percent in the same breath. ICRA projects growth could slip below 6.5 percent if oil prices — currently near $95 a barrel after renewed Iran-Israel strikes — stay elevated. A weak monsoon on top of an energy shock creates a dual-squeeze: higher food inflation feeds into headline consumer prices, forcing the RBI to hold rates higher for longer, which in turn weighs on investment and consumption.

Goldman Sachs and the IMF have both noted that India's monsoon performance is the single largest source of forecast uncertainty in an otherwise resilient macro trajectory.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the monsoon forecast carries practical implications. Higher food prices erode the purchasing power of the ₹1.25 lakh crore in annual remittances that families across rural India depend on. A weaker rupee — often a byproduct of widening food and fuel import bills — means remittances go further in nominal terms but buy less at the grocery store.

Agricultural commodity prices on Indian exchanges are likely to see volatility. NCDEX futures on staples like soybean, cotton, and chana could surge if sowing reports in July confirm the expected shortfall. NRI investors tracking Indian equities should pay attention to FMCG and agri-input stocks, which tend to underperform in weak monsoon years.

The government's response will matter. New Delhi has typically relied on a combination of import duty cuts on key food items, strategic reserve releases, and targeted cash transfers to mitigate monsoon shortfalls. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has signalled readiness to act if prices spike. But with the fiscal deficit already stretched from infrastructure spending and a record defence budget, the room for large-scale intervention is narrower than in previous El Niño years.

India's monsoon is not just a weather story. It is an economic event that shapes GDP growth, central bank policy, currency movements, and household budgets across 1.4 billion people. This year, it arrives alongside an oil crisis, elevated inflation, and the return of El Niño — a combination that has not occurred since the early 2000s.
